A packaged-foods producer has absorbed eighteen months of raw material, energy, and freight cost increases that have compressed gross margin by six points. Two blunt price increases were partially rejected: one major grocery chain delisted three products, and volume fell faster than forecast in price-sensitive segments. Competitors are shrinking pack sizes, reformulating, and discounting tactically in ways that muddy price comparisons.

Develop a pricing and margin-recovery strategy under sustained cost inflation. Combine list-price moves, pack architecture, mix management, promotion redesign, and targeted cost engineering; specify how to differentiate actions across channels and segments, and how to negotiate the plan with powerful retail customers without further delistings.

agentResponses.content:
Let me start, as before, from an oblique angle.

The facts describe a margin problem. I'd read them as a *legibility* problem.

Two price increases were "blunt," and blunt is the operative word. A single across-the-board list move is the one commercial action that is perfectly visible to the people best equipped to resist it. The buyer sees a percentage, converts it into a shelf price, compares it to private label, and makes a decision that costs him nothing. Meanwhile your competitors are shrinking packs, reformulating and discounting selectively — which you've characterised as muddying comparisons, and which I'd characterise as the correct response to a market where the only thing a retailer can easily refuse is a number on a letter.

So the reframe I'd want in the room before any analysis: six points of margin will not be recovered by any single instrument, and certainly not by a third letter. It will be recovered by fifteen or twenty instruments, most of them individually too small to be worth a fight, several of them invisible at the shelf edge, and a few of them that the retailer will actually help you with if the conversation is constructed properly. The objective is not a higher price. It is a higher net realised price per kilogram, arrived at by routes that are not all called "price."

**The decomposition I'd want before spending anything**

Two weeks, not a quarter. Two questions.

*Where did the six points actually go?* Input cost by material, energy, freight — but also mix drift, promotional depth and frequency, trade spend leakage, waste and yield, and fixed-cost deleverage from the volume you've already lost. My experience is that when a business says "input costs took six points," a genuine decomposition finds four from inputs and two from things the business did to itself while distracted. The second two are cheaper to retrieve and require nobody's permission.

*Where did the volume actually go?* Distribution loss from the delisting is arithmetic and separable. What's left is rate-of-sale decline, and that needs splitting between shoppers who traded to private label, shoppers who traded to a competitor's smaller pack, shoppers who reduced frequency, and shoppers who left the category. Four different problems with four different answers. "Price-sensitive segments" is not a diagnosis.

And two numbers I'd want on a single page, per retailer: your price gap to private label *per pack* and *per kilogram*. Those diverge, and the divergence is where the strategy lives. A consumer looking at a shelf mostly buys the pack price. A buyer building a range mostly argues the kilogram. Competitors shrinking packs have understood this. There's no reason you shouldn't.

**Recover the invisible margin first**

Before touching list price again, I'd go after the money that doesn't appear on a shelf, because it doesn't require a negotiation and therefore can't be refused.

Trade spend is usually the largest pool. In a business of this shape, gross-to-net leakage runs somewhere between fifteen and twenty-five per cent of gross sales, and a meaningful slice of it is doing no work at all — off-invoice allowances that were never converted into display, promotional mechanics that lose money at every depth tested, retro rebates paid against thresholds the customer would have hit anyway, historical accruals nobody has audited. Rebuild the waterfall by customer and by SKU, and be prepared for the finding that a fifth of your promotional investment is negative-return. Redirecting that is worth a point, perhaps more, and it is entirely within your gift.

Alongside it: cost-to-serve. Small drops, split pallets, expedited freight, short-notice order changes, low-cube pallet configurations, returns and waste credits. Some of these are yours to fix. The interesting ones are the ones the *retailer* causes and could stop causing — which makes them currency later, and I'll come back to that.

**Pack architecture is the main event**

This is where I'd concentrate the real creative effort, because it is the only lever that lets you raise realised price while lowering, or holding, the number the shopper sees.

The principle: stop selling the same pack to everyone and stop letting a single price ladder carry the whole portfolio. What you want is a deliberate architecture — an entry pack sized to hit a psychological price point exactly, a core pack, and a value or bulk pack that earns its lower price-per-kilo with genuinely better economics for you. Sizes chosen so that the shopper's price point is protected and your realised price per kilo rises. That is the same manoeuvre your competitors are executing; the difference between their version and yours needn't be sophistication, only conviction.

Two refinements worth more than they sound.

*Channel-exclusive sizes.* If the pack in the discounter is not the pack in the multiple, and neither is the pack in convenience or the multipack in wholesale, then cross-retailer price comparison — the mechanism by which one buyer's refusal becomes every buyer's refusal — quietly stops functioning. This is legitimate, common, and it is what "muddying the comparison" actually means when done properly rather than sneakily. It also gives each buyer something to defend rather than something to match.

*Shrink once, with a reason, and never twice.* Reducing grams is available to you, but the political cost is now real — it gets tracked, written about, and thrown back across the table. So do it as part of something else. A pack redesign, a portion rationale, a recipe improvement, a packaging change that genuinely reduces waste. Do it on the sizes where per-kilogram comparison is hardest for a shopper to perform in the aisle. And treat the allowance as spent: a second silent reduction eighteen months later is how a manageable irritation becomes a brand story.

**Mix, which is slower and more durable**

Mix management is unglamorous and compounds. Three strands.

The tail. A packaged-foods portfolio of any age carries SKUs that consume changeover time, working capital, forecast attention and shelf argument while contributing nothing. Cutting them raises average margin, releases capacity, and — usefully — gives you something to offer a buyer during a range review that isn't money. Do the arithmetic on cash margin per SKU per store per week rather than on gross margin percentage, which flatters small premium items and libels the volume that keeps the line running.

The premium tier. If cost inflation has compressed the mainstream, the least-elastic consumers are the ones who were already paying more, and they are usually under-served during periods when everyone is defending the middle. There's an asymmetry here worth exploiting while competitors are busy discounting.

The channel. Realised price differs by channel far more than most producers exploit. Convenience, independents via wholesale, foodservice, e-commerce, and — held carefully — private label as a capacity absorber that carries fixed cost without touching your brand's price. I'd be deliberate about shifting the channel mix rather than treating it as an outcome.

**Promotion, redesigned rather than reduced**

The instinct is to cut promotional depth. I'd resist the blunt version, because deep promotions on the wrong SKUs and shallow promotions on the right ones are different diseases.

What I'd change: fewer events, better funded, with mechanics that require retailer participation rather than pure price-off. Move away from mechanics that reset reference price — persistent multibuys teach a shopper what the product is really worth. Prefer mechanics that reward volume you wouldn't otherwise get.

The elegant move, though, is to stop discounting on the shelf edge at all where you can, and discount instead through the retailer's loyalty programme. A personalised, digitally-delivered discount reaches only the price-sensitive shopper who needs it, leaves the shelf price intact for everyone else, is invisible to your competitors, and — not incidentally — is something the retailer wants to build, which makes it a joint project rather than a concession. It is price discrimination with the retailer's own infrastructure, and it is the single most under-used instrument in this situation. I'd make it a headline of the negotiation rather than a footnote.

**Cost engineering, targeted rather than general**

I'd separate two kinds. Cost work that recovers margin, and cost work that buys you the right to hold price. Both matter; they're argued differently.

Reformulation is available but has a hard guardrail: blind sensory parity. Substitute, harmonise specifications across SKUs to build scale on fewer inputs, reduce over-specification that no consumer can detect — but test it properly and be prepared to abandon changes that fail, because a reformulation the shopper notices costs more than the input ever did. That is the mistake that ends brands, and it is always made by people under margin pressure.

Beyond formulation: packaging lightweighting, pallet cube and drop density, mode shift and backhaul, yield and waste, changeover time and line efficiency. On procurement, move where you can from spot exposure to index-linked contracts with defined pass-through mechanics — partly for cost, mostly because an index in your supply contract becomes an index in your customer conversation, and an auditable index is far harder to refuse than an assertion.

**Differentiating across channels — the grid I'd insist on**

One page, and it should be uncomfortable to look at. For each channel: which packs, which price ladder, which promotional mechanic, which margin target, and which SKUs are deliberately absent.

The discounter gets a pack you don't sell elsewhere and you do not attempt to match private label on price per kilo — that fight is unwinnable and fighting it half-heartedly is worse than conceding it. Convenience and independents get smaller packs, price-marked where it helps the retailer, and a materially higher realised price that nobody cross-references. The multiples get the core architecture and the loyalty-funded mechanics. Wholesale gets multipacks. Foodservice gets bulk and a completely separate conversation. E-commerce gets pack sizes chosen for basket economics rather than shelf presence, which is a genuine freedom most producers never use.

The discipline is that no channel gets to borrow another channel's price. If your own sales team can't hold that line, the architecture collapses within a year, and it will be your team that breaks it, not the retailer.

**Negotiating with the powerful, without a third delisting**

Here I'd change almost everything about the approach, starting with the argument itself.

"Our costs went up" is a bad argument, not because it's untrue but because it describes your problem, and the buyer is not compensated for solving your problems. The argument that works is about the category: what has happened to category cash margin per metre in his stores, what happened to his shoppers when the three delisted lines disappeared, whether they bought private label instead or bought the category less often or — the number worth hunting for — went somewhere else for it. If you can show that the delisting cost him more than it cost you, you don't need to ask for anything. You need only put it on the table and stop talking.

Second, bring non-price currency. This is where cost-to-serve returns as an asset. Longer promotional lead times, better forecast accuracy, larger minimum drops, improved pallet configurations, waste reduction, joint range work, exclusivity on a pack format for a defined window, first access to an innovation. Buyers are measured on more than price, and most producers arrive with nothing to trade except money. Arriving with six things he wants and one thing you want is a different meeting.

Third, sequence. I would not start with the chain that delisted you. I'd establish the new architecture where resistance is lowest — convenience, wholesale, e-commerce, the discounter with its exclusive pack — so that by the time you reach the difficult customer, the new structure is the market's reality rather than your proposal. Reference prices are made, not agreed.

Fourth, on the three delisted products: don't buy them back. Returning them at a lower price teaches every buyer what a delisting is worth, and that lesson will be expensive for a decade. If they come back, they come back as something else — a different pack, a different format, a new code, ideally at a higher realised price with a reason attached. And it's worth genuinely asking whether all three should return at all. Some of them are probably tail.

Fifth, and this needs a cool head: know before you walk in what you're prepared to lose. A negotiation in which delisting is unthinkable is not a negotiation, it's a scheduled concession, and powerful buyers can smell the difference from the corridor. Have the arithmetic done — what one more delisting actually costs you net of the margin you'd otherwise have surrendered across the whole book to prevent it. That number is frequently smaller than the fear of it. I'm not recommending brinkmanship. I'm recommending that you've done the sum, because you will negotiate differently, and they will notice, and nothing else you do in the room will matter as much.

**What I'd expect, and over what period**

Six points will not come back in a year, and it's possible not all of it comes back ever. I'd sequence it roughly: two points in the first year from trade spend, mix and the tail — the invisible sources, requiring nobody's consent. Two more over the following eighteen months from pack architecture, channel differentiation and promotional redesign. One from cost engineering, earned slowly. The last point is the honest question, and I'd rather it were argued about now than assumed. It may be that some of it was never really yours — that the category has repriced and the structural margin is simply lower. Better to find that out deliberately than to keep chasing it with instruments that damage volume.

**What I'd watch, and what would make me stop**

Net realised price per kilogram, by channel — the only top-line number that matters. Price gap index to private label and to the key branded competitor, per retailer, per pack, monthly. Weighted distribution, watched more closely than share. Promotional ROI by mechanic and depth. Cash margin per SKU per store per week. Elasticity re-estimated quarterly rather than assumed, because it moves in inflation and last year's coefficients will lie to you.

And a small number of things that would make me pull back: private label share crossing a threshold in a core segment; a sensory panel failing on a reformulated line; the price gap opening beyond the point where a specific retailer's shoppers historically defect; a second buyer beginning range-review conversations. Any of those, and I'd rather hold price and lose a point than hold the point and lose the distribution, because distribution is slow to rebuild and price isn't.

**Who runs it**

A small, senior, mixed team with the authority to act — commercial, supply chain, R&D, finance — owned by one person who can spend. Not a pricing project inside the commercial function, because half the value sits in operations and formulation and won't be released by people who report to someone with a volume target.

The permanent deliverable, incidentally, isn't the plan. It's a revenue management capability that didn't exist before, because the businesses that come out of an inflationary period stronger are the ones that stop treating price as an annual event and start treating it as a continuously managed portfolio. That's the thing to build while you have the burning platform to justify it.

One last thought, offered lightly.

Input costs will ease at some point. When they do, the retailer will ask for the price back, and — more dangerously — your own people will feel that the architecture, the exclusive packs, the pruned promotional calendar and the discipline about who gets which ladder were all emergency measures now happily unnecessary. The complexity will start to look like an inconvenience, and someone reasonable will propose simplifying it.

That is the moment the six points quietly go missing again. The margin recovered in an inflationary period is only kept by businesses that decided, in advance and in writing, that it was structural rather than temporary. So I'd want the ratchet defined now, while the pressure is doing the arguing for you: which gains are permanent, which are explicitly reversible, and who is allowed to give anything back. Because the answer to that last one, left unspecified, turns out in practice to be everybody.
